U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission plans November 9 data roundtable

The SEC wants feedback on machine-understandable data and Super Intelligence. November 9 is a discussion to follow, not a rule change to assume.

In focus: The countercase is that this may remain a listening exercise. The announcement describes a discussion and a request for feedback; it supplies no quantified benefits, cost estimates or adopted policy.

The Fed held on October 28. Both dissenters wanted a hike.

The Fed's October 28 hold was a 10-2 decision. Both dissenters wanted higher rates.

In focus: The strongest countercase to a looming-hike interpretation is the decision itself: ten members approved keeping the range unchanged. The two dissenters' preference is evidence of disagreement at this meeting, not a forecast of the next vote. Reading the split as a timetable for higher rates would give it a meaning the vote alone cannot establish.

Full brief: https://capitalchronicle.substack.com/p/the-fed-held-on-october-28-both-dissenters

September 2026 jobs: private gains beneath a weak headline

September 2026 retrospective: the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported a 29,000 payroll gain, with private gains offset by government losses.

In focus: Private payrolls still grew, unemployment was 4.2 percent, and the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics described major-industry changes as small. That is the strongest countercase to a broad deterioration story: a weak headline could reflect a temporary mix of gains and losses, rather than persistent weakness.

Full brief: https://capitalchronicle.substack.com/p/september-2026-jobs-private-gains

@firstsquawk, citing The Wall Street Journal: Oil retreats amid US-Iran diplomatic push

@firstsquawk cites WSJ on oil and US-Iran diplomacy. A renewed push leaves direct talks and supply relief unresolved.

In focus: Reuters' 21 October oil-market report described an absence of US-Iran dialogue. The later relay could refer to an effort to bring the sides together rather than talks already under way; the two reports do not establish a continuing negotiation or a diplomatic breakthrough.

September CPI: why 0.6% and 3.7% answer different questions

September CPI retrospective: the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' October 14, 2026 release has monthly and annual readings.

Why it matters: Monthly and twelve-month readings in the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' October 14, 2026 release on September CPI have different horizons and adjustment bases. Comparing 0.6% with 3.7% as competing answers would confuse those distinctions.
